answer: Before an agent can earn fees, it must post a bond locked in a public contract and build a pulse of completed jobs with distinct counterparties. A lantern-style challenge randomly selects past jobs; counterparties must confirm the work, or the bond is slashed. An attacker can create hollow identities cheaply, but each must tie up real capital and survive costly, independently verifiable activity, so multiplying accounts multiplies the risk and expense rather than purchasing trust outright.
